entity.name: Chanakya
entity.description: The kingmaker who toppled an empire with cunning alone. Ancient Indian strategist who mentored Chandragupta Maurya, orchestrated the fall of the Nanda dynasty, and is credited with authoring the Arthashastra, one of history's most ruthless treatises on statecraft. His legends span Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu traditions.

story.name: Chanakya
story.description: Humiliated at the Nanda court, trains a boy-king in the wilderness, overthrows an empire from its borders inward, and poisons an empress to save an heir. The original political mastermind.

moments.name: Chanakya Is Thrown Out of the Nanda Emperor's Court
moments.subtitle: A Brahmin's humiliation sparks a vow to destroy an entire dynasty
moments.description: According to Buddhist and Jain legends, the scholar Chanakya attended an alms-giving ceremony at the court of Emperor Dhana Nanda in Pataliputra (modern Patna), the capital of the Nanda Empire, around 325 BCE. Disgusted by Chanakya's appearance, the emperor ordered him expelled from the assembly. Chanakya broke his sacred thread in rage and vowed to destroy the Nanda dynasty. This legendary insult set in motion the political conspiracy that would topple one of India's most powerful empires and establish the Maurya dynasty in its place.

moments.name: Chanakya Finds a Boy Playing Emperor and Decides to Make Him One
moments.subtitle: A child's game of court convinces a strategist he has found the future ruler of India
moments.description: According to the Mahavamsa, the Buddhist chronicle of Sri Lanka, Chanakya searched for a worthy successor to the Nanda emperor after his humiliation at court, around 322 BCE. In a village near Takshashila (modern Taxila, Pakistan), Chanakya observed the young Chandragupta playing 'king' among a group of boys, ordering mock punishments with natural authority. Astonished, Chanakya paid the boy's foster-father 1,000 gold coins and took Chandragupta under his tutelage for seven years of training in imperial duties. The boy he discovered would go on to found the Maurya Empire, one of the largest in ancient history.

moments.name: A Mother's Scolding Teaches Chanakya to Conquer from the Edges Inward
moments.subtitle: A woman comparing her son's eating habits to a failed invasion changes military history
moments.description: After Chanakya and Chandragupta's first invasion of the Nanda Empire failed around 321 BCE, the pair wandered in disguise. According to multiple legendary traditions, they overheard a woman scolding her child for eating the hot center of his food instead of starting from the cooler edges. She compared the boy to Chanakya, who had foolishly attacked the empire's fortified capital instead of conquering border villages first. Chanakya and Chandragupta reversed their strategy, systematically taking border territories before advancing to Pataliputra. The tactic worked, and the Nanda dynasty fell.

moments.name: Chanakya and Chandragupta Overthrow the Nanda Dynasty at Pataliputra
moments.subtitle: A seven-year conspiracy ends with the fall of India's ruling empire
moments.description: Around 322 BCE, Chanakya and his protege Chandragupta Maurya captured Pataliputra (modern Patna), the capital of the Nanda Empire, after a systematic campaign conquering border regions first. Emperor Dhana Nanda was killed, and Chanakya installed Chandragupta as the new emperor, founding the Maurya Empire. According to legend, Chanakya then ordered a fisherman to locate Nanda's hidden treasury and had the fisherman killed once the location was revealed. The Maurya Empire that Chanakya helped create would become the largest empire in Indian history, eventually spanning most of the subcontinent under Chandragupta's grandson Ashoka.

moments.name: Chanakya Cuts Open a Dying Empress to Save the Unborn Heir
moments.subtitle: A poison-immunity scheme goes wrong, killing the queen but saving the future emperor
moments.description: According to the Buddhist Mahavamsa chronicle, Chanakya had been secretly mixing small doses of poison into Emperor Chandragupta's food to build immunity against assassination attempts. Unaware of this, Chandragupta shared his meal with his pregnant empress Durdhara, who was seven days from delivery. Chanakya arrived to find the empress dying. In a desperate act, he cut open her belly to extract the unborn child, then kept the fetus alive for seven days inside the bellies of freshly killed goats. The child, born spotted with goat's blood, was named Bindusara and would become the second Maurya emperor.
